Lighting for a 3D scene

Source: R/lights-3d.R
light_3d.Rd

Combines light sources with an ambient term and sets how the light changes face colours. Without light sources the scene has the lights of preset; the default preset has one directional light, light_directional(), from the upper left of the camera. See material_3d() for specular highlights.

Usage

light_3d(
  ...,
  ambient = NULL,
  mode = NULL,
  range = NULL,
  neutral = NULL,
  shadow_colour = "#1d2b53",
  highlight_colour = "#fff1d6",
  linear = NULL,
  material = NULL,
  viewer = NULL,
  preset = "default"
)

Arguments

...

Lights made with light_directional(), light_point(), light_head() or light_hemisphere(). None gives the lights of preset.

ambient

Uniform ambient light: a nonnegative strength (a grey) or one colour. NULL takes the preset's.

mode

Colour operation: "multiply", "tint", "lightness", "tone", "overlay", "soft" or "value". NULL takes the preset's.

range

Moves at full shadow and full highlight, c(shadow, highlight) with -1 <= shadow <= 0 <= highlight <= 1: fractions of the way to black and white in OKLab lightness for "lightness" and in HSV value for "value", to the tone colours for "tone", blend strengths for "overlay" and "soft". NULL takes the preset's when mode is the preset's mode, else c(-0.45, 0.3) for "lightness" and c(-0.6, 0.6) otherwise.

neutral

Angle in degrees, in [0, 180), between the normal and the light at which a signed mode leaves the colour unchanged. NULL takes the preset's when mode is the preset's mode, else 45.

shadow_colour, highlight_colour

Tone colours of "tone".

linear

Whether "multiply" and "tint" work in linear light (TRUE) or on encoded sRGB values (FALSE). NULL takes the preset's.

material

A material_3d() for the shaded layers that set none, or NULL for the preset's (plain Lambert reflection when the preset has none).

viewer

NULL, or the distance of the eye that the specular highlight is computed for, in radii of the sphere around the panel box, measured from the camera target along the view axis (OpenGL's local viewer; rgl places it at 1 / sin(fov / 2)). A near eye draws a highlight out along a surface. NULL takes the preset's, else the camera's eye (infinitely far under orthographic projection).

preset

Starting lighting: "default", "ggcube", "matplotlib", "rgl", "plotly" or "mathematica".

Value

A lighting configuration for coord_3d(). The backends that take one directional light (the path tracer and the raymarch backend) use the first directional light.

Details

preset starts from the lighting of another package; every argument given explicitly replaces the preset's value, and lights given in ... replace its lights.

  • "default": one light_directional(), ambient 0.35, mode = "lightness", range = c(-0.45, 0.4), neutral = 60.

  • "ggcube": ggcube's light(): a light along c(-0.5, 0, 1) in the data axes and its "hsv" mode at contrast = 1, i.e. mode = "value", range = c(-1, 1), neutral = 90.

  • "matplotlib": the shading of matplotlib's plot_surface(): the colour scaled by 0.65 + 0.35 * cos with the light at LightSource(azdeg = 225, altdeg = 19.4712) in the data axes, i.e. mode = "value", range = c(-0.7, 0), neutral = 0.

  • "rgl": the light of a new rgl scene, a white directional light at the eye (position (0, 0, 1) in eye coordinates, as rgl.attrib() reports; light3d()'s own default is 15 degrees above the eye), with rgl's default material (no ambient reflection, white specular, shininess 50) lit at the vertices (lighting = "vertex") on encoded values, and OpenGL's local viewer at rgl's default eye distance (viewer = 1 / sin(15 degrees), for its 30-degree field of view), as desktop rgl's fixed-function OpenGL does.

  • "plotly": plotly's surface lighting defaults: ambient 0.8, diffuse 0.8, the light at lightposition = (10, 10000, 0), which its shader takes in camera coordinates (straight above the viewer), and specular 0.05 with roughness 0.5 approximated by a Blinn exponent of 6, on encoded values.

  • "mathematica": Mathematica's Lighting -> Automatic: ambient RGBColor[0.4, 0.2, 0.2] and four coloured directional lights fixed to the image, shining from ImageScaled points {2, 0, 2}, {2, 2, 3}, {0, 2, 2} and {0, 0, 2} toward its centre, on encoded values. It suits light fills; Mathematica itself switches to white lights when a colour function is given.

mode sets how the light changes a face colour. "multiply" scales the colour by the ambient and diffuse light and "tint" scales its distance from white; both only darken, so a shaded fill no longer matches its legend key, and with the default light, which comes from near the viewer, the faces that face the camera all receive almost the same light. The signed modes darken faces turned from the light and lighten faces turned toward it, which keeps the colour readable against its key (Szafir et al. 2016; Kovesi 2015) and separates the faces that face the camera; the default is the signed mode "lightness". Each light gives a level in [-1, 1] from the angle between the normal and the light: 0 at neutral degrees, 1 facing the light and -1 facing away, linear in the cosine on each side (ggcube's ramp_smooth()). The levels are averaged over the lights, weighted by their luminance, and scaled by the material's diffuse strength. A level of 0 leaves the colour unchanged.

  • "lightness" moves the OKLab lightness (Ottosson 2020) toward black by up to the fraction abs(range[1]) in shadow and toward white by up to range[2] in light, and keeps the hue; where the moved colour leaves the sRGB gamut, its chroma is reduced until it fits (ggcube's tone_lightness()).

  • "tone" moves the colour in OKLab toward shadow_colour or highlight_colour, up to the fractions abs(range).

  • "overlay" and "soft" are matplotlib's LightSource blend modes on the encoded colour, with an intensity of 0.5 + level * abs(range) / 2.

  • "value" scales the HSV value of the encoded colour toward 0 by up to the fraction abs(range[1]) in shadow and moves it toward 1 by up to range[2] in light, keeping hue and saturation (ggcube's "hsv" mode).

multiply and tint work in linear light. With linear = FALSE they work on the encoded sRGB values instead, with the light colours and ambient taken as encoded values too and the light reaching a face capped at 1, as the fixed-function OpenGL pipeline, rgl, plotly and Mathematica do; the result is darker in the half shadow.

Specular highlights of material_3d() are added on top in every mode. Lightness-monotone palettes such as viridis lose the most under shading; isoluminant or diverging palettes combine best with relief shading. guide_colourbar_3d(), guide_coloursteps_3d(), guide_bins_3d() and guide_legend_3d() show the shaded colours of a key.

References

Szafir, Sarikaya, Gleicher (2016). Lightness constancy in surface visualization. IEEE TVCG 22, 2107-2121. doi:10.1109/TVCG.2015.2500240

Kovesi (2015). Good colour maps: how to design them. https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.03700

Ottosson (2020). A perceptual color space for image processing. https://bottosson.github.io/posts/oklab/

Examples

light_3d(light_head(), light_hemisphere("lightblue", "brown"), ambient = 0.1)
d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25), y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25))
d$z <- with(d, exp(-(x^2 + y^2)))
ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(x, y, z = z, fill = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(shading = "smooth", colour = NA) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral") +
  coord_3d(light = light_3d(light_directional(), mode = "lightness"))
ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85", shading = "smooth", colour = NA) +
  coord_3d(light = light_3d(preset = "mathematica"))
